sections.text: The end and the beginning of beings are unknown. We see only the intervening formations. Then what cause is there for grief?
One hears of the Spirit with surprise, another thinks It marvellous, the third listens without comprehending. Thus, though many are told about It, scarcely is there one who knows It.
Be not anxious about these armies. The Spirit in man is imperishable.

We have completed discussion on Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishadha Yoga, in which we have seen our conditions in this world. Arjuna Vishada Yoga represents our life where we are trained all our life for something. We have certain ideals and certain duties which we have held very dear to us. This is the very goal of my life.
But then sometimes the situation overwhelms us, which makes us confused about what is right and what is wrong. And at that point our mind starts giving us wrong indications of what is right and what is wrong. And we come up with all kinds of arguments about why I shouldnt be doing my duty, why I shouldnt be doing what I thought all this time that this is right for me.
And these arguments are sometimes so convincing that we convince ourselves, saying this is the voice of my antaratma, my inner conscience. However, it is just the blabbering of my mind, because I have not really established myself in my own true self. So this is not advice from Krishna, the consciousness in me, but rather my mind coming up with a defensive mechanism for why I shouldnt be doing this -- just because Im overwhelmed by the situation. So we have seen in the last few verses of chapter one, Arjuna put forth a very brilliant argument about why he shouldnt be fighting this war.
First he says, from my personal point of view, I shouldnt be fighting this war. To kill my own kith and kin looks very logical -- why should you be killing your kith and kin? When that argument didnt seem to be convincing Krishna, because he didnt have an approving reaction, Arjuna realized -- well, those kith and kin are standing right in front of you to kill you. So that didnt seem like a very logical argument, he goes to the next level and says the war itself is very evil.
Any war is evil because in war men will die -- many men will die, which is obvious. And therefore it will upset the entire equilibrium of society by destroying family units. When a man dies in the family, obviously the family loses the head of the household.
Now the women will be unprotected. And when the women become unprotected, they will do things which are not according to their dharma, because they have no protection. And when that happens, the whole system will be out of balance, giving rise to Varna Sankara -- intermixing of social classes -- in the next generation.
And that will completely upset our system, where the lineage of a father to the son in the same tradition will be giving oblation to the Pitrus. So the whole system will be completely destroyed according to Arjuna. Again, this makes a lot of sense, that war is evil.
Everyone knows war is not something which is to look forward to, but war is inevitable sometimes to protect the society, protect the dharma. So Arjuna makes all the arguments he thinks he can make against fighting this war, and then he sits down in his chariot. In the last verse, which we have seen, Sanjaya described that after making his argument, Arjuna didnt see any reaction from Krishna, so he drops down and throws his weapons away.
That means he does not even have a mental capacity to hang on to himself. So the next chapter which we are entering into, called Sankhya Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge. Yoga of Knowledge, in the line of the knowledge of the Sankhyas. Commentary, in our system there are six schools of thought, six different lines of philosophy, each one taking a slightly different route from the others.
Sankhya is one of them. Sankhya is supposed to be the most logical thought, almost as scientific as the modern sciences. Its a very logical approach to what is reality, what is truth, what is my essence, and what is the ultimate reality.
It takes a very logical approach, and as we have seen in Logic of Spirituality, it takes you through who am I and what is my self. Then where did I come from? Where we have seen anything which we see is an effect of a cause. When I see a book here, its an effect.
The cause is somebody who knew how to write the book, how to print the book, and how to put it together. The book is in front of me. So there are causes to cause any reality.
I exist, Im an effect. There are causes which cause me to be in this effect. Those causes are broadly defined as an efficient cause and a material cause.
Someone who knew how to create me in this effect. And someone also had the material to create me. Someone who knew how to create this book and someone also the material to create this book.
So the knowledge is called efficient cause and the material is called material cause. These two have to come together for any effect to come into existence. And we can trace back all of that.
And who had this efficient cause and material cause, both of them, to create this universe and me. And we trace it back to one entity who had the knowledge to create this universe and also had the material to create it. The efficient cause we call God -- God has the knowledge to create this universe, including my own self.
He also had the material to create this universe and myself. Then where did that material come from? At the end of our inquiry, we come to the conclusion that the material could not have come from anywhere else but from His own self, because nothing else existed before this universe was created -- only that one singularity which we call God. And that God had the knowledge.
The only material available to him was his own self. So out of his own self is created this universe. So my own self also cannot have come other than from his own self.
So myself and his self is one and the same. My self is nothing but the reflection of his self. Thus logically concluding that Myself cannot be separate from his self because his self is immortal, imperishable, Myself also cannot be perishable or mortal.
That is the philosophy of Sankhya. Now, the Sankhya philosophy here is not put together verbatim, but its flavor and essence were taken here by Bhagavan Vedvyasa, also called Badarayana, in the Uttar Mimamsa school of thought -- which is theistic, -- which accepts the reality of the one eternal self called Brahman, and also accepts the reality of this world and its relationship to Brahman. Thus, in Bhagavad Gita from Chapter 2 onward, we will see the synthesis of all three paths of realization explained in the Vedas: Bhakti Yoga (path of devotion), Karma Yoga (path of action), and Jnana Yoga (path of knowledge).
Bhagavad Gita puts all three yogas together as a comprehensive path of realization. Its Pravritti Vada -- you have to actively engage in this world, and then achieve the ultimate happiness youre seeking, with freedom from all the bondages and limitations you have superimposed on yourself. So in this second chapter, the teaching begins with Sanjayas assessment of whats happening there.
Chapter 2, verse 1 says Sanjaya Vacha tam tatha krupaya vistam asrupurna kulekshanam Vishidantam Idam Vakyam Uvacha Madhusudhana, Madhusudana Krishna. And we have seen the Madhusudana one who is the slayer of the demon Madhu. In the Puranic story, these are all demons Krishna has slain.
But philosophically, the demon Madhu represents that which seems very sweet to me in life but is not good for me -- that which is Preyas but not Shreyas, that which seems pleasant but is not truly good. Madhusudana is the slayer of that. When my intellect is awakened, I realize this may seem good to me, but is not good for me.
So Lord Krishna, Madhusudana, said this to the one who was completely overwhelmed by pity and despondency, his eyes full of tears, agitated. Arjuna had presented his case for why he shouldnt be fighting, and he was obviously expecting that Krishna would say, Well, lets not fight this war. But the reaction that came in the next two verses is completely shocking to Arjuna. Sri Bhagavan Uvacha -- the second verse, the first time Bhagavan speaks in this Gita: Kutastva Kasmalam Idam Vishame Samupasthitam, Anarya Jushtam Asvargyam Akirtikaram Arjuna.
O Arjuna, where does this weakness of heart come upon you? Which is Anari Jistham only practiced by those who are not civilized like you. Because Arya is the civilized one, Anaria is the uncivilized one according to their social order. One who is not civilized, who does not know the value of dharma, value of performing his own duties.
Once a duty is assigned to me, I have assigned myself as taking upon that role, then it becomes imperative that I perform that duty. Once I decide that I want to be a husband, all the duties of husbands are now superimposed on my and as long as I want to be a husband, I have to perform all those duties that the civilized mans law. Once I decide I want to be a father, all the fatherly duties are assigned to me and there is no escape for me to perform those duties.
Thats a civilized way of living. So once I have decided Im going to be the general of this army, the leader of this society, then all the duties assigned to me as the leader of this army and leader of this society, I have to perform those duties. Now when Im trying to shirk away from those duties.
That is Anaria jistham. Only those who are not civilized will do that. They will be those deadbeat dads.
They are not civilized. They do not know that their duty is to pay whatever the alimony for their children. So only the uncivilized one will do that.
So Bhagavan said, where does this Anaria jistham, weakness of your heart, which is not allowing you to do your duty, come upon you, which is a kirtikaram? Its not going to give you a good name. You may have all the good arguments to not do your duties, but once you dont do your duties, its not going to give you a good name, not going to make you famous. That how he ran away from his duties, you know, and this is because of the weakness of your heart.
When you were thinking correctly, you knew what your duty is because you are the leader of this army and you knew what to do is to fight the enemy which is standing in front of you. You have not asked for this war. You didnt decide that this is the right thing to do.
But the others in in their evil thoughts have decided to fight this war. Now it is your duty to lead your army into this war. So this is not something Krishna approves of -- running away from your duty.
Therefore, in the next verse he says: this is what you should be doing. Get up, O Parantapa! -- which is another name for Arjuna, meaning scorcher of the foes -- reminding him that his enemies are afraid of him. His training and achievement in life have been such that enemies tremble to stand in front of him.

Verse 28 presents a humbling truth: The end and the beginning of beings are unknown. We see only the intervening formations. Then what cause is there for grief? We witness only the middle portion of existence - a beings appearance in this world - without knowing where it came from before birth or where it goes after death. Our grief arises from the illusion that this visible portion is all there is.
Verse 29 acknowledges the rarity and wonder of this knowledge: One hears of the Spirit with surprise, another thinks It marvellous, the third listens without comprehending. Thus, though many are told about It, scarcely is there one who knows It. This is not discouraging but realistic - Self-knowledge is not easily attained. Many hear these teachings as mere philosophy; few truly realize them. And verse 30 brings closure to the argument: Be not anxious about these armies. The Spirit in man is imperishable.
Today, reflect on your relationship with this teaching. Do you hear it with surprise - as something new and intriguing? Do you think it marvellous - intellectually fascinating? Or do you listen without comprehending - the words going in but not transforming your life? The gap between hearing about the immortal Self and knowing it as your lived reality is the journey of spiritual practice. What would it take to move from intellectual understanding to direct experience? Consider that every moment of genuine self-inquiry - asking Who am I? and waiting for the answer - brings you closer to that realization.
